roles.name: Exec Sponsor / Board
roles.short: Accountable for the organisation's overall risk posture and for resourcing governance properly.

roles.name: Governance Lead
roles.short: Owns the governance programme day to day — frameworks, committee, registers, and reporting.

roles.name: Legal / DPO
roles.short: Lawfulness, data protection, and the point where AI obligations meet GDPR.

roles.name: ML / Data Science
roles.short: Builds and operates the models. Closest to training data, evaluation, and real system behaviour.

roles.name: Product Owner
roles.short: Owns an AI-enabled product or feature and the decisions it makes about people.

roles.name: Security
roles.short: Robustness, access, logging, and the security of models and the data behind them.

roles.name: Head of People / HR
roles.short: AI literacy, workforce impact, and AI used in recruitment or employment decisions — an Annex III high-risk area.

roles.name: Internal Audit
roles.short: Independent assurance that the controls described actually operate.

questions.text: We have a named executive owner accountable for AI Act compliance.
questions.help: One person, by name, not a committee and not "the CTO's team". If something went wrong tomorrow, this is who the board would call. If two people would both say "not me", answer No.
questions.evidence: A board minute, terms of reference, or role description naming the individual and the accountability.

obligation.label: Accountability for provider / deployer duties
obligation.detail: Obligations attach to the organisation, but supervisors expect a named accountable person who can answer for them.

questions.text: AI governance is a standing agenda item at a committee that minutes its decisions.
questions.help: A recurring forum with terms of reference, a quorum, and written minutes. Ad-hoc conversations, however senior, do not count — the evidence is the minute, not the meeting.
questions.evidence: Committee terms of reference plus the last two sets of minutes showing AI decisions taken.

obligation.label: Organisational governance arrangements
obligation.detail: Demonstrable oversight is what turns a written policy into an operating control.

questions.text: We know which role we play for each system — provider, deployer, importer, or distributor.
questions.help: Build it yourself and put your name on it, you are likely a provider. Use someone else's tool, you are likely a deployer. The obligations differ sharply, and you can be both for different systems. Fine-tuning or rebranding a third-party model can make you a provider.
questions.evidence: The role determination recorded per system in the AI inventory, with the reasoning.

obligation.label: Operator role determination
obligation.detail: Every other obligation depends on which role you occupy for that system.

questions.text: We have assessed which parts of the Act apply given our EU market exposure.
questions.help: The Act reaches you if you place a system on the EU market, or if its output is used in the EU — regardless of where you are established. Being outside the EU is not by itself an exemption.
questions.evidence: A written scope assessment covering EU market placement and where system output is used.

obligation.label: Territorial scope
obligation.detail: Extra-territorial reach catches output used in the EU, not only EU establishment.

questions.text: Every AI system in use or development is captured in a central inventory.
questions.help: One list, owned by a named person, covering built, bought, and embedded AI — including AI features switched on inside SaaS you already licence. If you cannot say where the list lives, answer No.
questions.evidence: The inventory itself, plus evidence of how it is kept current (intake gate, discovery sweep).

obligation.label: Knowing what you operate
obligation.detail: You cannot comply for systems you cannot list. Inventory underpins every other obligation.

questions.text: Each system is classified by risk tier — prohibited, high-risk, limited, or minimal.
questions.help: Classification is a decision with a date and an owner, recorded against the system. "We think most of ours are low risk" is not a classification.
questions.evidence: Classification recorded against each system with a date, an owner, and the rationale.

obligation.label: Risk classification
obligation.detail: The tier determines which obligations apply and by when.

questions.text: General-purpose AI models we build or integrate are identified, with their obligations mapped.
questions.help: Covers foundation models you train and, more commonly, commercial LLMs you build on. Integrating GPAI into a product can pull you into provider duties for the resulting system.
questions.evidence: A list of GPAI models in use, mapped to the obligations each attracts.

obligation.label: GPAI obligations
obligation.detail: GPAI carries its own documentation, copyright, and systemic-risk duties.

questions.text: The inventory records purpose, data sources, model or vendor, and lifecycle stage.
questions.help: A list of system names is not an inventory. The test: could you answer a regulator's "what does it do, on what data, from whom, and is it live?" without going to ask around.
questions.evidence: Inventory export showing the fields populated for a sample of systems, not just the headers.

obligation.label: Technical documentation inputs
obligation.detail: These fields are the minimum feed into Annex IV technical documentation.

questions.text: We have confirmed that no system performs a prohibited practice.
questions.help: Social scoring, manipulative or exploitative techniques, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference in workplaces or schools, and most real-time remote biometric identification in public. This needed to be true from February 2025.
questions.evidence: A completed prohibited-practice screen per system, signed off and dated.

obligation.label: Prohibited practices
obligation.detail: In force since 2 February 2025 and carrying the highest penalty tier. There is no transition period left to rely on.

questions.text: We screen new use cases against the prohibited list before development starts.
questions.help: A gate at intake, not a review at launch. The point is to stop work before money is spent, so it must sit early enough that someone can still say no.
questions.evidence: The intake process document plus screening records for recent new use cases.

obligation.label: Preventive screening
obligation.detail: Catching a prohibited use at launch means the cost is already sunk.

questions.text: High-risk systems have a documented risk management process across the lifecycle.
questions.help: Continuous, not a one-off sign-off: identify, evaluate, mitigate, then keep checking once the system is live and its inputs drift.
questions.evidence: A risk assessment per high-risk system, with review dates that have actually been met.

obligation.label: Risk management system
obligation.detail: A continuous, documented process running the whole system lifecycle.

questions.text: Data governance for training, validation, and test data addresses relevance, representativeness, and bias.
questions.help: Do you know where training data came from, whether you may lawfully use it, who it does and does not represent, and what you did when you found a skew?
questions.evidence: Data documentation covering source, licence, representativeness testing, and bias findings.

obligation.label: Data and data governance
obligation.detail: Training data quality is an explicit, testable high-risk obligation.

questions.text: Technical documentation is maintained and current for each high-risk system.
questions.help: Annex IV sets out what it must contain. The failure mode is not absence but staleness — documentation written at launch and never touched again.
questions.evidence: Technical documentation per Annex IV, with a version history showing it is maintained.

obligation.label: Technical documentation
obligation.detail: Must exist before market placement and stay current afterwards.

questions.text: Systems automatically log events sufficient for traceability.
questions.help: Machine-generated logs, retained long enough to reconstruct what a system did and why on a given date. Application logs often do not capture the model inputs and outputs that actually matter here.
questions.evidence: Log configuration and a retention policy, plus a sample log proving inputs and outputs are captured.

obligation.label: Record-keeping
obligation.detail: Automatic logging over the system lifetime, sufficient to trace behaviour.

questions.text: Human oversight measures are designed in and genuinely operable by real people.
questions.help: The honest test: can the named human actually understand the output, and do they have the authority, time, and confidence to override it? A reviewer approving 400 decisions an hour is not oversight.
questions.evidence: Oversight design documentation, override statistics, and the reviewer's training record.

obligation.label: Human oversight
obligation.detail: Oversight must be effective in practice, not merely present in the design document.

questions.text: Systems meet expected accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity levels, with evidence.
questions.help: Declared metrics with test results behind them, including behaviour under adversarial input and on edge cases. "It performed well in testing" without numbers is a No.
questions.evidence: Test results with declared metrics, subgroup performance, and adversarial testing evidence.

obligation.label: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligation.detail: Appropriate levels declared and evidenced across the lifecycle.

questions.text: A conformity assessment route is identified and planned before the applicable deadline.
questions.help: Know whether your route is self-assessment or a notified body, and how long it takes. Notified-body capacity is finite and the queue will not be shorter closer to the deadline.
questions.evidence: A conformity assessment plan naming the route, the body if applicable, and the target date.

obligation.label: Conformity assessment
obligation.detail: Annex III high-risk obligations apply from December 2027; Annex I from August 2028.

questions.text: Post-market monitoring and a serious-incident reporting process exist.
questions.help: Someone watches live performance, and there is a defined path — with a clock on it — for reporting serious incidents to the relevant authority.
questions.evidence: The monitoring configuration and a documented incident reporting procedure with named owners.

obligation.label: Post-market monitoring and incident reporting
obligation.detail: Serious incidents carry short reporting deadlines once identified.

questions.text: People are told when they are interacting with an AI system.
questions.help: Clear at the point of interaction, not buried in terms of service. Applies to chatbots and AI-driven assistants unless it is obvious to a reasonable person.
questions.evidence: Screenshots or UI evidence of the disclosure at the point of interaction.

obligation.label: Transparency to natural persons
obligation.detail: Applies from August 2026, with a grace period running to December 2026.

questions.text: AI-generated or manipulated content is marked or watermarked.
questions.help: Synthetic audio, image, video, and text intended to inform the public must be machine-readably marked. This includes marketing material your teams generate.
questions.evidence: Marking or watermarking configuration, plus samples of generated content showing it applied.

obligation.label: Marking of synthetic content
obligation.detail: Machine-readable marking of AI-generated or manipulated content.

questions.text: Emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, if used, is disclosed to affected people.
questions.help: If you use neither, answer Not applicable. Note that emotion inference in workplaces and education is prohibited outright, not merely restricted.
questions.evidence: Disclosure notices, or a documented confirmation that neither technique is used.

obligation.label: Emotion recognition disclosure
obligation.detail: Disclosure duty where permitted; outright prohibition in workplace and education contexts.

questions.text: For GPAI we use, we hold provider documentation and understand training-data transparency expectations.
questions.help: Do you actually have the model documentation from your vendor, or do you just assume it exists? "It is on their website" only counts if someone has read it and filed it.
questions.evidence: The provider documentation you actually hold on file, not a link to a vendor website.

obligation.label: GPAI provider documentation
obligation.detail: Downstream deployers rely on provider documentation to meet their own duties.

questions.text: Vendor contracts flow down AI Act obligations and evidence rights.
questions.help: Right to obtain documentation, to be told about material model changes, and to audit or receive assurance. Standard SaaS terms almost never include these unless you asked.
questions.evidence: Executed contracts or amendments containing the AI clauses, for your critical vendors.

obligation.label: Contractual flow-down
obligation.detail: You remain accountable for systems you deploy but did not build.

questions.text: Where personal data is involved, a DPIA or equivalent assessment is completed and linked.
questions.help: AI Act compliance does not discharge GDPR. High-risk AI touching personal data will almost always need a DPIA, and the two assessments should reference each other rather than sit in separate drawers.
questions.evidence: The completed DPIA, the DPO's recorded opinion, and its cross-reference to the AI assessment.

obligation.label: DPIA / fundamental rights impact assessment
obligation.detail: GDPR duties run in parallel, and certain deployers owe a fundamental rights impact assessment.

questions.text: Staff who build, buy, or operate AI have AI literacy appropriate to their role.
questions.help: A live obligation since February 2025, and one of the few that applies to everyone regardless of risk tier. The 2026 Omnibus softened it: you must take measures to SUPPORT the development of AI literacy, not guarantee any individual reaches a particular level. Proportionate to role — a procurement lead needs different literacy from an ML engineer.
questions.evidence: Training completion records by role, plus the syllabus showing it is role-appropriate.

obligation.label: AI literacy
obligation.detail: In force since 2 February 2025 and applicable across the organisation. Amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 to an effort-based duty: take measures to support AI literacy, rather than ensure it.

questions.text: A current data governance framework defines ownership of data domains.
questions.help: Named owners for each significant data domain, not just a platform team who happen to host the tables.
questions.evidence: The framework document plus a domain list with named owners who know they hold the role.

obligation.label: Data governance foundation
obligation.detail: AI data quality obligations rest on ordinary data governance underneath.

questions.text: Data is classified by sensitivity, with handling rules for each class.
questions.help: People need to know what they may paste into an external AI tool. Without a classification scheme, that judgement gets made individually and badly.
questions.evidence: The classification policy and evidence of labels applied in at least one production system.

obligation.label: Data classification and handling
obligation.detail: Underpins both confidentiality controls and lawful AI input.

questions.text: We measure data quality against defined dimensions and thresholds.
questions.help: Completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency, validity, uniqueness — with thresholds and a named owner who acts when one is breached.
questions.evidence: Quality reports against defined thresholds, showing measurement over several periods.

obligation.label: Data quality
obligation.detail: Training and test data must be relevant, representative, and to the extent possible free of errors.

questions.text: A risk register captures AI and data risks with owners and treatment plans.
questions.help: Risks with named owners, agreed treatments, and review dates — not a spreadsheet last updated at the previous audit.
questions.evidence: The risk register, with owners, treatment plans, and evidence of review at committee.

obligation.label: Risk register
obligation.detail: The operational record of the Art. 9 risk management system.

questions.text: There is a defined process for logging and responding to AI incidents.
questions.help: People know what counts as an AI incident, where to report it, and what happens next. Test it: could a support engineer name the process?
questions.evidence: The incident procedure plus the incident log, including at least one worked example.

obligation.label: Incident management
obligation.detail: Serious incidents must reach the authority within short, defined windows.

questions.text: Decision rights and escalation paths are documented and understood.
questions.help: Who can approve a high-risk deployment, who can halt one, and what happens when two functions disagree. The real test is whether it has survived a live disagreement.
questions.evidence: The decision rights matrix, plus a real escalation that followed it.

obligation.label: Deployer governance
obligation.detail: Unclear escalation is the most common reason controls fail in practice.

questions.text: A RACI or equivalent makes governance responsibilities explicit.
questions.help: Each significant activity has exactly one accountable party. Two accountable parties means nobody is.
questions.evidence: The RACI, validated so every row has exactly one accountable party.

obligation.label: Allocation of responsibilities
obligation.detail: Documented accountability is the first thing assurance looks for.

questions.text: Model documentation exists for material models, covering intended use and limitations.
questions.help: A model card or equivalent: what it is for, what it should not be used for, how it performs across groups, and its known failure modes.
questions.evidence: Model cards for material models, covering intended use, limitations, and subgroup performance.

obligation.label: Model documentation
obligation.detail: Feeds both technical documentation and deployer instructions for use.

questions.text: Controls are mapped to obligations, with named owners and assurance evidence.
questions.help: A control library that links each obligation to the control that satisfies it, who owns it, and how you would evidence it operating.
questions.evidence: The control library mapping obligations to controls, with owners and test results.

obligation.label: Quality management system
obligation.detail: Providers of high-risk systems need a documented quality management system.

questions.text: Internal Audit or an equivalent independent function reviews AI governance.
questions.help: Independent of the people who built and run the systems. A second-line review is valuable but is not the same as independent assurance.
questions.evidence: An audit report or assurance plan covering AI, produced independently of the delivery teams.

obligation.label: Independent assurance
obligation.detail: Boards increasingly expect third-line coverage of AI risk.

questions.text: The board receives regular, structured reporting on AI and data governance.
questions.help: A recurring pack with risk posture, movement since last time, and explicit decisions being asked for — not an occasional verbal update.
questions.evidence: The last two board packs, showing risk posture and decisions sought.

obligation.label: Board oversight
obligation.detail: Demonstrable board engagement is a common supervisory expectation.

questions.text: We track KPIs and KRIs that show whether governance is actually working.
questions.help: Coverage, quality, incident, and readiness measures with a trend. Activity counts such as "policies published" tell you nothing about effectiveness.
questions.evidence: A metrics pack with trend over at least three periods, not a single snapshot.

obligation.label: Monitoring effectiveness
obligation.detail: Post-market monitoring needs measures, not anecdotes.

questions.text: AI used in recruitment, performance, or other employment decisions is identified and governed.
questions.help: CV screening, interview scoring, performance ranking, and workforce allocation are Annex III high-risk uses. Answer Not applicable only if you are certain no such tool is in use anywhere, including inside your HR SaaS.
questions.evidence: The inventory entry, risk assessment, and DPIA for each employment-related AI system.

obligation.label: Employment and worker management
obligation.detail: Employment-related AI is expressly high-risk under Annex III.

questions.text: Staff have clear, current guidance on acceptable use of AI tools at work.
questions.help: Practical and specific: which tools are approved, what may never be pasted into them, and who to ask. If people are quietly using unapproved tools, the guidance has already failed.
questions.evidence: The published guidance, the approved tool list, and evidence staff can find both.

obligation.label: AI literacy in practice
obligation.detail: Literacy obligations are met through usable guidance, not a policy nobody reads.

questions.text: Security controls cover model and training-data specific threats.
questions.help: Prompt injection, training-data poisoning, model extraction, and unintended disclosure through outputs. Conventional application security does not cover these by default.
questions.evidence: Threat model or security test results covering injection, poisoning, and extraction.

obligation.label: Cybersecurity of AI systems
obligation.detail: Art. 15 expects resilience against AI-specific attack classes.

data-governance-framework.title: Data Governance Framework
data-governance-framework.purpose: The reference that defines how your organisation governs data: what data you hold, who owns it, what quality is expected, and how decisions about it are made. It is the foundation the AI governance work sits on — most AI failures trace back to a data problem nobody owned.
data-governance-framework.evidence: An approved framework with named owners for every data domain.

ai-governance-framework.title: AI Governance Framework
ai-governance-framework.purpose: A single reference that defines how your organisation governs AI across its lifecycle — who is accountable, what principles apply, how risk is tiered and controlled, and how it connects to data governance and the EU AI Act. It is the document you hand to a board, a regulator, or a new hire to explain "how we do AI here".
ai-governance-framework.owner: Governance lead, ratified by the committee
ai-governance-framework.evidence: An approved framework, with risk tiers and lifecycle gates agreed.

governance-charter.title: Governance Charter
governance-charter.purpose: A short, board-approved mandate that establishes the governance programme: why it exists, what authority it has, what it covers, and how success is measured. It is what you point to when someone asks "who says so?".
governance-charter.evidence: A board-approved mandate naming the sponsor and the authority to halt.

maturity-assessment.title: Maturity Assessment
maturity-assessment.purpose: A structured baseline of how capable your governance actually is today, across the dimensions that matter, so you can prioritise honestly and show movement over time.
maturity-assessment.evidence: A dated baseline score with evidence against each dimension.

data-governance-policy.title: Data Governance Policy
data-governance-policy.purpose: The mandatory rules for handling data. Where the framework explains how governance works, this policy states what people must and must not do, in language you can hold someone to.
data-governance-policy.evidence: A published policy with numbered, enforceable statements.

data-quality-standard.title: Data Quality Standard
data-quality-standard.purpose: Defines what "good enough" data means in measurable terms — the dimensions, how they are measured, the thresholds that apply, and who acts when a threshold is breached.
data-quality-standard.evidence: Thresholds set and measured on your two most important domains.

data-classification-policy.title: Data Classification & Handling Policy
data-classification-policy.purpose: Defines the sensitivity tiers your data falls into and the handling rules for each — including the rules that decide what may be pasted into an AI tool.
data-classification-policy.evidence: A published scheme with the AI-input rules staff can find.

acceptable-ai-use-policy.title: Acceptable AI Use Policy
acceptable-ai-use-policy.purpose: The staff-facing rules for using AI at work: what is encouraged, what needs approval, and what is never allowed. This is the most-read document in the kit, and usually the one that prevents the most damage.
acceptable-ai-use-policy.evidence: A one-page policy staff have attested to, with an approved-tool list.

ai-development-standard.title: AI Development & Deployment Standard
ai-development-standard.purpose: The engineering-facing requirements for building, testing, deploying, and operating AI systems — the technical controls that make the framework's principles real inside a delivery pipeline.
ai-development-standard.evidence: Lifecycle gates enforced in the pipeline, producing evidence.

third-party-ai-risk-policy.title: Third-Party AI Risk Policy
third-party-ai-risk-policy.purpose: How you assess, contract for, and monitor AI you did not build — including AI features that appear inside software you already licence. For most organisations this is the majority of their AI exposure.
third-party-ai-risk-policy.evidence: An assessment on file for every critical AI vendor.

raci.title: RACI Matrix
raci.purpose: Removes ambiguity about who does what. For every significant governance activity it names exactly one accountable party, so decisions have an owner and gaps become visible before they become incidents.
raci.owner: Governance lead, agreed in a room
raci.evidence: One accountable party per activity, confirmed by the people named.

committee-charter.title: Committee Charter (Terms of Reference)
committee-charter.purpose: Establishes the forum where governance decisions are actually made: its authority, membership, quorum, cadence, and what it must decide rather than merely discuss.
committee-charter.evidence: Terms of reference with quorum and the right to halt a system.

roles-responsibilities.title: Roles & Responsibilities
roles-responsibilities.purpose: Defines each governance role in enough detail that it can be put in a job description, recruited for, and assessed against — rather than assumed.
roles-responsibilities.evidence: Named holders who know they hold the role.

decision-rights.title: Decision Rights & Escalation
decision-rights.purpose: States who can decide what, at what threshold, and what happens when people disagree or a decision is needed urgently. It is the document that stops governance stalling.
decision-rights.evidence: A decision matrix tested against a real past decision.

data-asset-register.title: Data Asset Register
data-asset-register.purpose: The catalogue of what data you hold, who owns it, how sensitive it is, and where it lives. Almost every other governance control depends on it.
data-asset-register.evidence: Your material data assets registered with owners and classification.

ai-system-inventory.title: AI System Inventory
ai-system-inventory.purpose: The single list of every AI system you build, buy, or have embedded in something you already licence. It is the foundation of AI Act compliance: every other obligation applies per system, so a system you have not listed is one you cannot govern.
ai-system-inventory.owner: Governance lead, with a discovery sweep
ai-system-inventory.evidence: Every AI system listed with a named owner, tier and rationale.

risk-register.title: Risk Register
risk-register.purpose: The live record of data and AI risks: what could go wrong, how likely and how bad, what you are doing about it, and who owns it.
risk-register.evidence: Risks written as cause-event-consequence, each with an owner.

incident-log.title: Issue & Incident Log
incident-log.purpose: The record of what went wrong, what you did, and what changed as a result. It is both a management tool and the evidence base for serious-incident reporting duties.
incident-log.evidence: A defined route people can name, plus the log itself.

processing-dpia-log.title: Processing & DPIA Log
processing-dpia-log.purpose: The record of personal data processing activities and the impact assessments that cover them — the point where AI governance meets data protection law.
processing-dpia-log.evidence: A completed DPIA with the DPO's recorded opinion.

ai-risk-assessment.title: AI Risk Assessment
ai-risk-assessment.purpose: A structured assessment of what could go wrong with a specific AI system, how bad it would be, and what you are doing about it. For high-risk systems it is the core evidence that Art. 9 risk management is operating.
ai-risk-assessment.evidence: A signed assessment with residual risk accepted at the right level.

model-card.title: Model Card / Model Risk Documentation
model-card.purpose: Standard documentation for a model: what it is for, what it was trained on, how well it performs and for whom, and where it should not be used. Feeds both AI Act technical documentation and the instructions deployers rely on.
model-card.evidence: Documentation covering intended use, limitations and subgroup results.

control-library.title: Control Library & Assurance Map
control-library.purpose: Maps obligations to the controls that satisfy them, names an owner for each, and records how you would evidence the control is operating. It turns "we have a policy" into "here is what we do and how you can check".
control-library.evidence: Obligations mapped to controls, each with an owner and evidence.

board-pack.title: Board Pack Template
board-pack.purpose: A structured report that gives the board what it needs to discharge its oversight duty: current posture, what changed, what went wrong, and what decisions are being asked of them.
board-pack.evidence: A pack the board reads, with the decisions being sought stated.

kpi-dashboard.title: KPI / KRI Dashboard
kpi-dashboard.purpose: The measures that show whether governance is actually working — coverage, quality, timeliness, and leading indicators of trouble — rather than how much documentation exists.
kpi-dashboard.evidence: A stable metric set with trend over at least three periods.

eu-ai-act-readiness-checklist.title: EU AI Act — 25-point readiness checklist
eu-ai-act-readiness-checklist.purpose: A fast self-assessment of where your organisation stands against the EU AI Act. Work through it, mark what is true today, and treat every unticked box as a backlog item.
eu-ai-act-readiness-checklist.evidence: A dated position against all 25 points.

eu-ai-act-timeline.title: EU AI Act timeline (2026 Digital Omnibus)
eu-ai-act-timeline.purpose: The dates that actually bind you, reflecting the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments — what is already in force, what was deferred, and what to work backwards from.
eu-ai-act-timeline.evidence: A roadmap working backwards from the binding dates.

bands.label: Advanced
bands.blurb: Controls are measured and independently assured. Focus on continuous improvement.

bands.label: Established
bands.blurb: The core is in place and operating. Focus on evidencing that controls work.

bands.label: Developing
bands.blurb: Foundations exist but coverage is uneven. Close the documentation and process gaps.

bands.label: Early
bands.blurb: Significant exposure. Start with inventory, prohibited-practice screening, and accountability.
